title: Statement on the publication of the Financial Stability Review 2026 of the Deutsche Bundesbank
summary: Michael Theurer argues that the resilience of the German financial system depends on whether institutions can continue to lend, settle payments and meet redemptions when several shocks arrive together. In his opening statement for the Bundesbank’s 2026 Financial Stability Review, he contrasts elevated equity and corporate-bond valuations with an export economy facing trade barriers, expensive energy and structural adjustment. Low risk premiums leave room for a sharp repricing if expectations change. He distinguishes an orderly correction, which can unwind overvaluation, from forced sales that propagate losses. He gives no date or probability for either outcome.

The pressure on corporate borrowers is already visible. Monthly insolvencies reached their highest level since 2014, and banks’ non-performing loans have increased since the middle of the previous year. Borrowers refinancing loans taken out when rates were low face an additional squeeze. Losses so far have been manageable. Chart 3 extends that observation with an adverse exercise in which industries including chemicals and automotive manufacturing come under greater structural strain. A significant number of banks, including some large institutions, would see substantially higher corporate credit losses. The exercise is a conditional stress test. Theurer cautions against assuming that every euro of reported capital buffer can absorb such losses while the institution continues lending. Other regulatory constraints can bind at the same time.

The household sector illustrates a different exposure. Aggregate debt is low relative to income and liquid resources. In the second quarter of 2026, however, just under 40% of newly originated residential mortgage volume financed more than 90% of the property value. Almost 11% financed more than the property was worth (Chart 4). These figures concern the flow of lending by value. A high-income household can service a highly leveraged purchase, but an income loss alongside a house-price decline makes a lender’s recovery less secure. The coincidence of those shocks matters more than either statistic alone.

Slower growth and higher debt-service burdens also limit fiscal support. Under unchanged policies, European Commission projections cited in Chart 5 take aggregate euro-area public debt from 88% of GDP in 2025 to 105% in 2036, with the higher-debt group near 140%. Theurer calls for early, gradual adjustment and growth-enhancing investment. A sovereign downgrade can hurt banks, insurers and funds holding the debt, and bank distress can feed back to the public balance sheet. Better bank capital and resolution arrangements have reduced some of that risk. He proposes concentration limits or capital surcharges on large exposures to individual sovereigns.

Liquidity links can amplify losses across funds. Open-ended German real estate funds have experienced withdrawals since mid-2023, and some suspended redemptions during 2026. More broadly, a fund facing redemptions can sell units in another fund, passing the cash requirement along. In a scenario modelled on the opening days of the Iran conflict in March, total fund-sector losses were almost twice initial losses and insurance-sector losses almost three times initial losses (Chart 6). Those ratios describe amplification under the assumed shock. They are neither forecasts nor a comparison of the sectors’ absolute losses. Direct aggregate German exposures to private credit appear limited but are concentrated, with major gaps on leverage and interconnections.

Theurer supports maintaining existing capital buffers, making them more usable, strengthening European reporting on funds and equipping supervisors to manage systemic liquidity risks. Shared dependence on critical third-party providers adds an operational dimension. AI can improve defensive monitoring while accelerating threats, making the continuity of payments and other shared services relevant to system-wide oversight. The proposed regulatory simplification is intended to preserve the capacity to absorb shocks.

questions.question: Which banks could actually release capital to maintain lending under the industrial stress scenario?
questions.detail: Reported capital ratios and large sector exposures are only a starting point. Seek bank-level Pillar 3 disclosures and supervisory stress assumptions to compare losses, binding constraints and usable headroom for lenders to automotive and chemical firms. A change in ranking would matter for subordinated credit and the borrowers dependent on those institutions.

questions.question: Where do fund redemptions generate the largest second-round sales?
questions.detail: The model shows a sizable amplification of initial losses but does not identify the marginal asset that would have to be sold in a new episode. Compare fund-of-funds holdings, insurer ownership, settlement dates, cash reserves and redemption restrictions in fund statements and supervisory statistics. This distinguishes assets with broad ownership from those with a small number of forced sellers.

questions.question: How exposed is the high-loan-to-value mortgage cohort to a joint income and house-price shock?
questions.detail: The new-lending shares reveal collateral risk but do not establish default probabilities. Mortgage vintage data with debt service, income and regional employment would help determine where thin collateral coverage coincides with fragile cash flow. A portfolio with strong borrowers and weak collateral can behave differently from one where both protections deteriorate together.
